Clinical Vignette: Linh

Linh was fifty-seven when she came to the clinic, her dark hair streaked with grey, her posture careful and contained. She had been designing residential interiors for nearly thirty years—a career built on the premise that spaces could be controlled, made beautiful, made safe. In March 2019, she had been in Barcelona on a work trip, meeting with a client about a penthouse renovation. She had stepped out of the hotel at dusk to walk to a nearby restaurant, her phone in one hand, her mind already on fabric swatches and lighting schemes. A van mounted the curb three metres ahead of her. She remembered the sound first—a terrible, metal-on-concrete shriek—then the scatter of bodies, the smell of hot rubber and something else, something acrid and chemical that would later be identified as residue from explosives. Thirteen people died that evening. Linh had been separated from the initial impact by chance and a few metres of pavement, but she had seen the bodies, had heard the screaming, had felt the heat of the blast wave against her face. She had smelled alcohol on a paramedic's breath as he led her away.

For the first weeks after returning home to Los Angeles, Linh had functioned. She returned to her office, attended meetings, spoke to her husband Marcus in measured tones about the trip. But something had fractured. Within a month, she had begun to notice that certain moments would crack open the careful surface she maintained. A photograph on her phone—one she had taken of the Barcelona street that afternoon, before—would appear in her camera roll and she would feel her chest tighten, her breathing shallow. The smell of alcohol, even from Marcus's evening drink across the room, would send her into a state of urgent, panicked energy. When a client asked her to describe what she had witnessed, to help them understand her absence from a project, the act of speaking the words aloud—the van, the bodies, the sound—had triggered something so overwhelming that she had excused herself and spent twenty minutes in her car, shaking.

These moments of being pulled back into the event had come to terrify Linh, and in her terror she had developed ways to manage the unbearable intensity. When a photograph surfaced or when she caught the scent of alcohol, the panic that followed would drive her to move—to run, to hurt herself in small controlled ways, to eat mechanically late into the night—anything to discharge the intensity before it consumed her entirely. She had learned, through painful repetition, that the moment she noticed a trigger—the smell of cologne with alcohol notes, a particular angle of light—she had to act immediately. If she did not run, did not hurt herself, did not eat, the panic would overwhelm her entirely, and so she had come to move the instant a trigger appeared, before the feeling could take hold. When a photograph surfaced or when she caught the scent of alcohol, she would respond with a kind of frantic physicality. She had begun to exercise obsessively, running for hours in the early mornings, pushing her body past fatigue into a state of numb exhaustion where the intrusive memories seemed, temporarily, to recede. She had also started hurting herself in small, private ways—pinching the soft skin of her inner arm until it bruised, pressing her fingernails into her palms—as though the controlled pain could somehow discharge the overwhelming feelings that threatened to break through. Late at night, she would eat large quantities of food, sitting alone in the kitchen, the mechanical act of chewing and swallowing a temporary anchor to the present moment. These strategies worked, in a narrow sense; they gave her something to do with the intensity. But they also seemed to feed something darker in her thinking.

Over the months that followed, Linh had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that safety was an illusion she had once naively accepted. Once she had settled into this conviction, almost anything could confirm it—the particular angle of a parked van, a stranger's proximity on the street, the quality of light at dusk—and each of these ordinary details would suddenly register as a warning, snagging her attention in ways they never had before. But her conviction did more than simply interpret what was already there; it actively generated new threats. Because she was certain the world was unsafe, she had begun to notice things she would once have dismissed—a delivery truck idling outside her studio, a man standing too close on the sidewalk, the metallic screech of brakes—and each of these details, filtered through her belief that danger was imminent, became a trigger in its own right. She had to be vigilant at all times—watching other people's faces, their hands, their proximity to her. In her design studio downtown, she found herself tracking the movements of her employees and clients with an intensity that exhausted her. She had come to feel that she could not manage even minor frustrations; a delayed email or a client's last-minute change request would trigger a cascade of anxiety that left her depleted for hours. This fragility, this sense that she was barely holding together, seemed to make her more vulnerable to the triggers themselves. She noticed that her hypervigilance—the constant monitoring, the sense that danger was imminent—actually seemed to make her notice things more acutely: the smell of someone's cologne that contained alcohol notes, the particular quality of light that resembled the Barcelona dusk. Living at that pitch of alertness, her nervous system had become so finely tuned to threat that it generated new triggers almost constantly—a car horn that sounded too much like metal on concrete, a stranger's raised voice, even the smell of her own perfume if it carried certain notes that reminded her of that evening. The constant state of threat her body maintained meant that ordinary stimuli—a door slamming, a siren in the distance, the particular way light fell at dusk—were no longer neutral; they had become dense with danger, each one a potential trigger waiting to detonate. The more she believed the world was dangerous, the more she saw evidence of danger everywhere, and the more she saw it, the more her body responded with the sensation that the bombing was happening again.

When she caught herself hurting her arm or found herself running until her legs burned, Linh would feel a crushing sense of shame and despair. These acts, meant to relieve the pressure, only seemed to reinforce her belief that she was fragile, that she could not cope, that something fundamental had broken inside her. The maladaptive coping itself became a trigger—proof, in her mind, of her own deterioration. Her marriage had begun to strain. Marcus would find her running in the dark at five in the morning, or he would catch her in the kitchen at midnight, surrounded by empty containers. He wanted to help, but when he touched her unexpectedly—a hand on her shoulder—she would flinch violently, her nervous system interpreting the contact as a threat. She had missed three major client presentations in the past year, citing illness. Her reputation, so carefully built, was beginning to fracture.

It was Marcus who finally insisted she seek help. She had come to the clinic because she was afraid—not just of the memories, but of what she was becoming, of the person her own coping mechanisms were turning her into. What frightened her most was the feeling that she was trapped in a cycle she could not escape, that each attempt to manage the overwhelming feelings only pulled her deeper into the belief that she was broken, that the world was unsafe, that she would never feel normal again.
